text: Mabo v Queensland (No 2) is a landmark High Court of Australia decision concerning native title and the status of Indigenous rights to land under Australian common law. The Court rejected the doctrine of terra nullius and held that the common law of Australia could recognise native title where Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples had maintained a connection with land according to traditional laws and customs. The case established that native title may survive the acquisition of sovereignty, although it may be extinguished by valid government acts inconsistent with the continued enjoyment of native title. The reasoning mattered because it shifted Australian land law away from the assumption that the continent was legally empty at settlement and recognised that pre-existing Indigenous rights could have legal effect within the common law. The case is central to property and constitutional law because it explains the relationship between sovereignty, radical title, common law recognition, and extinguishment.

Donoghue v Stevenson established the modern foundation of negligence. The plaintiff alleged that she became ill after consuming ginger beer containing a decomposed snail. Although she had no contract with the manufacturer, the House of Lords held that a manufacturer may owe a duty of care to the ultimate consumer where harm is reasonably foreseeable. Lord Atkin's neighbour principle stated that a person must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions which can reasonably be foreseen as likely to injure persons who are closely and directly affected by those acts. The case matters because it separated negligence liability from contract and created a general method for identifying duties of care. It is commonly used to explain foreseeability, proximity, and the emergence of a general duty of care framework.

case_name: Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co
text: Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co is a leading contract law case on unilateral offers. The defendant advertised that it would pay a reward to anyone who used the smoke ball as directed and still contracted influenza, and stated that money had been deposited to show sincerity. The Court of Appeal held that the advertisement was not mere puff because it showed an intention to be bound. It was a unilateral offer to the world, capable of acceptance by performance. Mrs Carlill accepted the offer by using the product as directed and contracting influenza. Consideration existed because she incurred the inconvenience of using the smoke ball and the company received the benefit of increased sales. The case is important for formation, intention, certainty, acceptance by conduct, and unilateral contracts.

case_name: Amalgamated Society of Engineers v Adelaide Steamship Co Ltd
text: The Engineers Case transformed Australian constitutional interpretation. The High Court rejected earlier doctrines of implied intergovernmental immunities and reserved state powers. The Court held that Commonwealth legislative powers should be interpreted according to the ordinary meaning of the constitutional text, read in context, rather than restricted by implications designed to preserve state autonomy. The reasoning mattered because it expanded the practical reach of Commonwealth legislative power and marked a move toward text-based interpretation. The case is a foundational authority in Australian constitutional law because it changed the balance of federal power and remains central to interpreting Commonwealth heads of power.

Lange v Australian Broadcasting Corporation confirmed the implied freedom of political communication under the Australian Constitution. The case arose in the context of a defamation claim by a former New Zealand Prime Minister. The High Court held that the Constitution requires freedom of communication about government and political matters because representative and responsible government depend on electors being able to receive and discuss political information. The Court reformulated the test for whether a law impermissibly burdens the freedom. The freedom is not a personal right but a restriction on legislative and executive power. The case is important because it connects the implied freedom to the text and structure of the Constitution and provides the framework for analysing burdens on political communication.

Wyong Shire Council v Shirt is a leading Australian negligence case on breach of duty. The High Court held that a risk is foreseeable if it is not far-fetched or fanciful. Once foreseeability is established, the court asks what a reasonable person would do in response to the risk. That assessment involves balancing the probability of harm, the seriousness of the possible injury, the burden of taking precautions, and the social utility of the activity. The case is important because it shows that foreseeability alone does not establish breach. The real issue is whether a reasonable person in the defendant's position would have taken precautions. It remains a foundational case for analysing breach in negligence.

Baltic Shipping Co v Dillon concerned contract damages following a cruise that was cut short when the ship sank. The High Court considered whether the plaintiff could recover damages for disappointment and distress as well as restitutionary recovery for the fare. The case is commonly studied for the limits of damages in contract and the circumstances in which damages for disappointment or distress may be available. The reasoning distinguishes ordinary commercial contracts from contracts directed toward enjoyment, relaxation or pleasure. The case is important because it illustrates how contract remedies protect the plaintiff's expectation interest, while also recognising that some contracts have non-financial purposes that may justify damages for disappointment.

Salomon v Salomon & Co Ltd established the principle of separate legal personality. Once a company is validly incorporated, it is a legal person separate from its shareholders, directors and controllers. Mr Salomon controlled the company, but the House of Lords held that the company was not his agent or trustee merely because he held most of the shares. The company's debts were its own, not automatically the debts of Mr Salomon personally. The case is foundational in company law because it explains limited liability, corporate personality, and the corporate veil. It is also the starting point for analysing when courts may or may not disregard the separate legal entity of a company.

Keech v Sandford is a foundational fiduciary duty case. A trustee held a lease for the benefit of an infant beneficiary. When the lessor refused to renew the lease for the beneficiary, the trustee obtained the lease for himself. The Court held that the trustee had to hold the renewed lease on trust for the beneficiary. The rule was strict: a fiduciary must not place themselves in a position of conflict or profit from their position without consent, even where the beneficiary could not have obtained the benefit personally. The case is important because it establishes the strict no-conflict and no-profit approach in equity, designed to deter fiduciaries from acting against the interests of those they serve.

Plaintiff S157/2002 v Commonwealth is a leading Australian administrative law case on jurisdictional error and privative clauses. The High Court held that a privative clause cannot protect a decision affected by jurisdictional error from judicial review. A decision involving jurisdictional error is not a decision made under the Act in the relevant legal sense. The case is important because it confirms the constitutional significance of judicial review and the supervisory role of courts in ensuring that administrative decision-makers remain within lawful authority. It is commonly studied for the relationship between statutory interpretation, migration decisions, jurisdictional error and the limits of legislative attempts to restrict review.

case_name: Codelfa Construction Pty Ltd v State Rail Authority (NSW)
text: Codelfa is a leading Australian case on contractual interpretation and frustration. The High Court held that surrounding circumstances may be considered to resolve ambiguity but not to contradict clear language. The contract was frustrated when an injunction prevented night work, fundamentally altering performance. The case is important for explaining the limits of interpretation and the doctrine of frustration.

case_name: Toll (FGCT) Pty Ltd v Alphapharm Pty Ltd
text: Toll v Alphapharm reaffirmed that a person who signs a contractual document is bound by its terms, regardless of whether they have read them, absent misrepresentation or other vitiating factors. The case is central to incorporation of terms and the objective theory of contract.

case_name: Ermogenous v Greek Orthodox Community of SA Inc
text: Ermogenous rejected rigid presumptions about intention in family or social arrangements. The High Court held intention is assessed objectively based on circumstances. The case is important for clarifying intention to create legal relations.

case_name: March v E & MH Stramare Pty Ltd
text: March v Stramare is a leading case on causation. The High Court rejected rigid 'but for' tests and emphasised common sense causation. It is central to understanding factual causation in negligence.

Rogers v Whitaker established that doctors must warn patients of material risks. The High Court held that professional standards do not determine duty conclusively. The case is central to medical negligence and duty of care.
Kioa v West confirmed that procedural fairness applies unless clearly excluded. The High Court emphasised fairness in administrative decision-making. It is foundational for natural justice.

case_name: Kirk v Industrial Court of NSW
text: Kirk confirmed that state courts must retain supervisory jurisdiction over jurisdictional error. It constitutionalised judicial review at state level.

case_name: Minister for Immigration and Citizenship v Li
text: Li clarified legal unreasonableness as a ground of review. A decision lacking an evident and intelligible justification may be invalid.

case_name: Hospital Products Ltd v US Surgical Corporation
text: Hospital Products clarified when fiduciary duties arise, distinguishing commercial relationships from fiduciary ones.
ASIC v Adler is a leading case on breaches of directors duties including acting in good faith and misuse of position.

Masters v Cameron is a leading Australian contract law case on whether parties intended to be immediately bound. The High Court identified categories of agreements made subject to a later formal contract. The case is important because it helps determine whether apparent agreement is already binding or merely conditional on execution of a later document.

case_name: Australian Woollen Mills Pty Ltd v Commonwealth
text: Australian Woollen Mills v Commonwealth is a leading case on offer and consideration. The High Court held that a government subsidy announcement did not necessarily amount to a contractual offer. The case is important because it shows that an act will only be consideration if it is performed in response to a promise and as the requested price of that promise.

case_name: BP Refinery (Westernport) Pty Ltd v Shire of Hastings
text: BP Refinery is a leading authority on implying terms in fact. The case sets out conditions commonly used to assess whether a term should be implied, including reasonableness, business efficacy, obviousness, clarity and consistency with express terms. It is central to Australian contract law on implied terms.

case_name: Perri v Coolangatta Investments Pty Ltd
text: Perri v Coolangatta Investments concerns contractual conditions and the time within which a condition must be satisfied. The High Court considered when a party may terminate where a condition remains unfulfilled. The case is useful for analysing conditional contracts, reasonable time for performance and termination rights.

Waltons Stores v Maher is a leading Australian case on equitable estoppel. The High Court held that a party may be restrained from departing from an assumption it induced where another party has relied on that assumption to their detriment. The case is important for pre-contractual dealings, unconscionability and reliance-based relief.

case_name: Commercial Bank of Australia Ltd v Amadio
text: Commercial Bank of Australia v Amadio is a leading case on equitable unconscionable conduct. The High Court held that a transaction may be set aside where one party is under a special disadvantage and the stronger party unconscientiously takes advantage of that position. The case is central to undue advantage, vulnerability and equitable intervention.

Perre v Apand is a leading Australian negligence case on pure economic loss. The High Court considered vulnerability, foreseeability, control and indeterminacy in determining whether a duty of care should be recognised. It is important because it shows that pure economic loss requires careful duty analysis beyond simple foreseeability.

Sullivan v Moody is a key case on novel duties of care. The High Court emphasised that negligence duties must be coherent with other legal obligations and statutory functions. The case is important because it prevents duty analysis from being reduced to foreseeability alone and requires attention to legal coherence.

case_name: Graham Barclay Oysters Pty Ltd v Ryan
text: Graham Barclay Oysters v Ryan concerns negligence claims against public authorities and private actors following contaminated oysters. The High Court considered the limits of public authority liability and the need to assess statutory powers, control and responsibility. The case is important for duty of care analysis involving regulators and public bodies.

case_name: Romeo v Conservation Commission of the Northern Territory
text: Romeo v Conservation Commission concerns breach of duty and obvious risks. The High Court considered whether a public authority was negligent for failing to fence or warn against a cliff risk. The case is important for assessing reasonable precautions, obvious dangers and the practical limits of occupier or public authority liability.

Vairy v Wyong Shire Council is a negligence case concerning injury from diving into shallow water. The High Court considered whether a council breached its duty by failing to provide warnings. The case is useful for breach analysis, obvious risks and the limits of reasonable precautions in recreational settings.

case_name: Adeels Palace Pty Ltd v Moubarak
text: Adeels Palace v Moubarak is a leading case on causation under civil liability legislation. The High Court held that even if a duty and breach are shown, the plaintiff must prove factual causation. The case is important because it demonstrates that security failures or risk precautions must be causally connected to the harm suffered.

Breskvar v Wall is a leading Torrens title case. The High Court described the Torrens system as a system of title by registration rather than registration of title. The case is important because it explains immediate indefeasibility and the central role of registration in Australian land law.

Bahr v Nicolay (No 2) concerns the interaction between Torrens title and equitable obligations. The High Court considered whether a registered proprietor who took title with notice of a prior arrangement could be bound in equity. The case is important for fraud, in personam claims and constructive trusts in Torrens land.

Wik Peoples v Queensland is a major native title case. The High Court held that pastoral leases did not necessarily extinguish all native title rights. Native title could coexist with pastoral lease rights to the extent of consistency, with lease rights prevailing in case of inconsistency. The case is central to native title and property law.

Boardman v Phipps is a leading fiduciary duty case. The House of Lords held that fiduciaries who profit from information or opportunities obtained through their fiduciary position may be accountable, even where they acted honestly and benefited the trust. The case illustrates the strictness of the no-profit rule.

Baumgartner v Baumgartner is a leading Australian constructive trust case. The High Court imposed a constructive trust where pooled contributions in a domestic relationship made it unconscionable for one party to retain the property beneficially. The case is important for remedial constructive trusts and equitable responses to unconscionable retention of property.

Muschinski v Dodds concerns constructive trusts arising from a failed joint endeavour. The High Court recognised that equity may intervene where it would be unconscionable for one party to retain a benefit after the basis of a joint arrangement has failed. The case is central to constructive trusts and equitable adjustment.

Corin v Patton concerns the requirements for an effective gift or transfer in equity. The High Court considered whether the donor had done everything necessary to transfer the interest. The case is important for voluntary assignments, gifts and when equity will recognise an incomplete transfer.

Commonwealth v Tasmania, known as the Tasmanian Dam Case, is a major constitutional law decision on the external affairs power. The High Court upheld Commonwealth legislation implementing international treaty obligations. The case is important because it confirmed the breadth of the external affairs power and its significance for Commonwealth legislative capacity.

Melbourne Corporation v Commonwealth established an implied limitation protecting the states from Commonwealth laws that discriminate against them or impair their capacity to function as governments. The case is central to federalism and the structural implications of the Constitution.

Roach v Electoral Commissioner concerns constitutional protection of the franchise. The High Court held that voting rights may be limited only for substantial reasons consistent with representative government. The case is important for understanding constitutional implications from representative democracy.

McCloy v New South Wales is a leading implied freedom case. The High Court adopted structured proportionality analysis for assessing whether a law that burdens political communication is justified. The case is important for modern implied freedom reasoning.

Ainsworth v Criminal Justice Commission is a key procedural fairness case. The High Court held that procedural fairness may be required where a decision or report affects a person's interests, including reputation. The case is important for understanding when fairness obligations arise.

Annetts v McCann is a leading procedural fairness case. The High Court held that natural justice applies where a decision may affect rights, interests or legitimate expectations unless excluded by clear statutory language. The case is commonly used to explain the breadth of fairness obligations.

case_name: He Kaw Teh v The Queen
text: He Kaw Teh v The Queen is a leading criminal law case on mens rea and statutory interpretation. The High Court considered whether fault should be required for a serious drug importation offence. The case is important because it shows the presumption that criminal offences generally require a guilty mind unless Parliament clearly indicates otherwise.

case_name: Woolmington v Director of Public Prosecutions
text: Woolmington v DPP is a foundational criminal law case on the burden of proof. The House of Lords held that the prosecution bears the burden of proving guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The case is commonly described as establishing the golden thread of criminal law.

Pfennig v The Queen is a leading evidence case on propensity and similar fact evidence. The High Court considered when evidence of other conduct is sufficiently probative to be admitted despite prejudicial risk. The case is important for understanding admissibility of tendency-like reasoning at common law.

IMM v The Queen is a major evidence case on probative value under the uniform evidence legislation. The High Court held that when assessing probative value, the court assumes the evidence is accepted and asks how strongly it could affect the probability of a fact in issue. The case is important for relevance, probative value and admissibility reasoning.

case_name: Aon Risk Services Australia Ltd v Australian National University
text: Aon Risk Services v ANU is a leading civil procedure case on case management and amendments. The High Court emphasised that delay, prejudice and the efficient use of court resources are relevant when deciding whether late amendments should be allowed. The case is important for modern procedural fairness, efficiency and litigation discipline.

R v Tang is a leading Australian criminal law case on slavery offences. The High Court considered the meaning of slavery in the Criminal Code and held that slavery can exist even without legal ownership where powers attaching to ownership are exercised over a person. The case is important for understanding statutory interpretation, exploitation, control, consent and the substance of criminal liability.

R v Lavender concerns criminal negligence manslaughter. The High Court considered the standard required for criminal negligence and whether the accused's conduct involved such a great falling short of the standard of care that punishment was warranted. The case is important for distinguishing civil negligence from criminal liability.

Pemble v The Queen is a leading criminal law case on intention and jury directions. The High Court held that the trial judge must leave open to the jury any defence or issue that arises on the evidence, even if not relied on by counsel. The case is important for criminal procedure, fair trial principles and the relationship between evidence and legal issues.

case_name: Zecevic v Director of Public Prosecutions (Vic)
text: Zecevic v DPP is the leading Australian common law authority on self-defence. The High Court reformulated the test around whether the accused believed on reasonable grounds that it was necessary to do what was done in self-defence. The case is important for homicide, defensive force and the interaction between subjective belief and objective reasonableness.

Dietrich v The Queen is a leading case on fair trial rights. The High Court held that, in serious criminal trials, where an accused is indigent and unrepresented through no fault of their own, a stay may be ordered if proceeding would result in an unfair trial. The case is important for procedural fairness, criminal justice and access to legal representation.

Papakosmas v The Queen is a leading evidence case under the uniform evidence legislation. The High Court considered the admissibility and use of complaint evidence in a sexual assault trial. The case is important because it explains relevance, hearsay, credibility and the statutory approach to evidence that may serve more than one purpose.

Smith v The Queen is a leading evidence case on opinion and identification evidence. Police witnesses gave evidence identifying the accused from photographs. The High Court held that the evidence was not admissible opinion evidence where the jury could make its own comparison. The case is important for relevance, opinion evidence and the limits of identification testimony.

Adam v The Queen concerns the use of prior inconsistent statements under the uniform evidence legislation. The High Court considered how evidence admitted for one purpose may be used and how the legislation altered common law limits. The case is important for hearsay, credibility and statutory evidence reasoning.

Hoch v The Queen is a leading case on similar fact evidence. The High Court emphasised that evidence of similar allegations must be treated cautiously where there is a real possibility of concoction or collusion. The case is important for understanding probative value, prejudice and safeguards against unfair reasoning.

Hughes v The Queen is a leading High Court case on tendency evidence. The Court considered when tendency evidence has significant probative value and how it may be used in sexual offence proceedings. The case is important for the uniform evidence law, tendency reasoning and the relationship between similarity, pattern and probative force.

case_name: Port of Melbourne Authority v Anshun Pty Ltd
text: Port of Melbourne Authority v Anshun is the leading authority on Anshun estoppel. The High Court held that a party may be prevented from raising a claim or issue in later proceedings where it was so connected with earlier proceedings that it was unreasonable not to raise it then. The case is central to finality, abuse of process and civil procedure.

case_name: State of Queensland v JL Holdings Pty Ltd
text: State of Queensland v JL Holdings concerned late amendments and case management. The High Court emphasised that the attainment of justice between the parties remained central, although later authority has placed greater weight on case management and efficiency. The case is often studied alongside Aon Risk Services v ANU to show the shift in procedural priorities.

case_name: Batistatos v Roads and Traffic Authority of NSW
text: Batistatos v Roads and Traffic Authority concerns abuse of process and delay. The High Court considered when proceedings may be permanently stayed because delay makes a fair trial impossible or the proceeding oppressive. The case is important for civil procedure, finality and the court's control over its own processes.

case_name: Tomlinson v Ramsey Food Processing Pty Ltd
text: Tomlinson v Ramsey Food Processing concerns issue estoppel and the finality of litigation. The High Court considered the effect of earlier decisions on later proceedings. The case is important for understanding res judicata, estoppel and when parties are prevented from relitigating matters.

D'Orta-Ekenaike v Victoria Legal Aid is a leading case on advocate immunity. The High Court confirmed immunity for work intimately connected with the conduct of a case in court. The case is important for legal ethics, professional negligence, finality of litigation and the administration of justice.

Giannarelli v Wraith is a major Australian case on advocate immunity. The High Court held that barristers were immune from negligence suits for work done in court and work intimately connected with court proceedings. The case is important for legal ethics, duties to the court and the administration of justice.

case_name: Clyne v New South Wales Bar Association
text: Clyne v New South Wales Bar Association is a leading professional discipline case. The High Court considered the conduct expected of barristers and the disciplinary jurisdiction over legal practitioners. The case is important for duties to the court, professional standards and protection of the administration of justice.

Foss v Harbottle is a foundational company law case on the proper plaintiff rule. The company is generally the proper plaintiff for wrongs done to it, and courts are reluctant to interfere with internal management where the majority can ratify the conduct. The case is important for derivative actions, shareholder litigation and corporate personality.

Gambotto v WCP is a leading Australian company law case on amendments to corporate constitutions affecting minority shareholders. The High Court held that expropriation of minority shares must be for a proper purpose and fair in the circumstances. The case is important for minority shareholder protection and limits on majority power.

Walker v Wimborne is a leading case on directors' duties in corporate groups. The High Court held that directors must consider the interests of the company of which they are directors, not simply the interests of a broader group. The case is important for separate legal personality, corporate groups and directors' duties.

court: New South Wales Court of Appeal
text: Daniels v Anderson is a leading Australian company law case on directors' and officers' duties of care. The NSW Court of Appeal held that directors must take reasonable steps to monitor company affairs and cannot remain passive. The case is important for corporate governance, board oversight and the standard of care expected of directors.

Greenhalgh v Arderne Cinemas is a company law case on majority power and alteration of articles. The Court considered whether powers were exercised bona fide for the benefit of the company as a whole. The case is important for shareholder voting, majority control and limits on constitutional amendment.

Chan v Zacharia is a leading Australian fiduciary duty case. The High Court held that fiduciary obligations may continue in relation to partnership property and opportunities during winding up. The case is important for the no-profit rule, conflict duties and fiduciary obligations in partnerships.

Warman International v Dwyer is a leading case on fiduciary remedies. The High Court considered the scope of an account of profits where a fiduciary misused an opportunity. The case is important because it explains how equitable remedies may be shaped to reflect causation, contribution and fairness while maintaining strict fiduciary standards.

case_name: Farah Constructions Pty Ltd v Say-Dee Pty Ltd
text: Farah Constructions v Say-Dee is a major Australian equity case. The High Court considered fiduciary duties, constructive trusts and accessorial liability under Barnes v Addy. The case is important for knowing receipt, knowing assistance and the discipline of Australian intermediate appellate courts following seriously considered dicta of the High Court.

Breen v Williams concerns the limits of fiduciary obligations in the doctor-patient relationship. The High Court declined to impose broad fiduciary obligations requiring access to medical records. The case is important because it distinguishes fiduciary duties from duties in contract, tort and statute, and shows that fiduciary law is not a general fairness doctrine.

Giumelli v Giumelli is a leading proprietary estoppel case. The High Court considered the appropriate remedy where a promise about land had been relied on to the claimant's detriment. The case is important because it shows that equitable relief should be proportionate and may be monetary rather than a direct transfer of property.

Frazer v Walker is a leading Torrens title case. The Privy Council confirmed immediate indefeasibility upon registration, even where registration followed a void instrument, subject to recognised exceptions such as fraud. The case is important for Australian property law because it underpins the security and conclusiveness of Torrens registration.

case_name: Mercantile Mutual Life Insurance Co Ltd v Gosper
court: New South Wales Court of Appeal
text: Mercantile Mutual v Gosper is an important Torrens title case concerning fraud and mortgage interests. The NSW Court of Appeal considered when fraud affects registered interests and how the knowledge or conduct of agents may matter. The case is useful for analysing the fraud exception to indefeasibility.

Parker v British Airways Board is a leading case on finders and possession. The Court considered the rights of a finder of lost property against the occupier of premises. The case is important for understanding possession, control, intention to exclude and priority between competing claims to found property.
